mappings.note: The Panchatantra's worldwide translation explained by its universal morals: an ancient Indian work (LO-161) whose reach abroad is India's contact with other regions (LO-173).
Finds Magh Bihu wrongly placed in Punjab among Uttarayan, Pongal and Lohri - the regional spread of one festival, so LO-166.
Travellers noticing turmeric and cumin across very different regional cuisines; the item names unity in diversity outright, which is LO-166.
Defines staple grains as the everyday cereals and pulses of a region - the common base beneath India's varied food, so LO-166.
European demand for chintz read as proof of Indian textile quality: India's craft contribution (LO-174) reaching markets outside India (LO-173).
Classifies the Ramayana and Mahabharata as epics; a fact about the literary works, so LO-161.
Rejects the claim that Makara Sankranti is kept identically everywhere while accepting its astronomical basis - the item turns on regional variation, hence LO-166.
One Sanskrit source and two hundred adaptations: a fact about the work (LO-161) used as the chapter's one-becomes-many figure (LO-166).
Matches Sita to the Ramayana against Rama-in-Mahabharata distractors; a personalities-in-literary-works item, squarely LO-161.
Names the People of India project as the survey of India's communities - the documentation of human diversity, so LO-166.
Rules out turmeric as a staple grain among rice, bajra and chana dal; the item tests the shared food base, so LO-166.
Statement set separating Pongal from kite flying and Lohri from Tamil Nadu - regional festival variation, mapped with the other festival items.
Identifies a museum's six-yard unstitched printed garment as a sari from its versatility and many drapes; the chapter's dress-diversity thread, so LO-166.
Sanskrit as the epics' original language - a fact about the literary works rather than about diversity.
The dhoti alongside the sari as unstitched draped cloth; a comparison inside India's dress tradition, hence LO-166.
Picks jowar as an Indian millet against quinoa, oats and buckwheat - again the shared staple base of LO-166.
Identifies a mid-January bonfire-and-feast festival as Lohri or Maghi; recognising a regional form of the shared harvest festival, so LO-166.
Patan Patola placed in Gujarat; a sari-to-region item, mapped with the other regional weave questions.
Rules out 'lengthy epic' from the Panchatantra's qualities, which needs the distinction between fable and epic - a literary-category point, so LO-161.
Accepts that tribes keep Ramayana legends but rejects that they adopt the Sanskrit text unchanged: the local variation is the point (LO-166), worked on an epic (LO-161).
Finds Paithani wrongly placed in West Bengal among Banarasi, Kanjivaram and Muga - regional textile traditions, so LO-166.
Statement set on the number of languages, the unstitched sari and Makara Sankranti's many names; three strands of the same diversity argument.
Identifies Diwali from rangoli, lamps and sweets, and notes it is kept across India and abroad - a shared festival across a diverse country, hence LO-166.
The epics probing right against wrong: their content (LO-161) and the dharma-and-adharma values they weigh (LO-175). Not LO-166, since nothing regional is at issue.
'The Many in the One' read as diversity strengthening a composite whole - the attitude clause of LO-166.
Recalls the 325-language count; a measure of India's human diversity, so LO-166.
Names Vincent Smith as the historian struck by bewildering diversity - the same observation as the multiple-choice version, under LO-166.
Names a cereal eaten across India; the shared food base of the diversity argument.
Names an Indian millet - bajra, jowar or ragi; the same shared-staple ground as the cereal item.
The sari as the unstitched garment worn across most of India - the common form behind hundreds of regional variations.
Names one famous silk sari; a regional weave, so LO-166 with the other textile items.
Defines a relief as a design raised from a panel - the vocabulary of the Vaishali sculpture used in this chapter as dated evidence, so LO-159 rather than the diversity outcome.
Names chintz as the printed cotton that took 17th-century Europe; India's craft contribution abroad, mapped with the other chintz items under LO-174.
Makara Sankranti marking the harvest season - the shared meaning behind the festival's many regional names.
Pongal as the Tamil Nadu name; a regional variant of the same festival, so LO-166.
Magh Bihu as the Assamese name for the mid-January harvest festival; the companion item to Pongal.
Names the Panchatantra as the animal-fable collection teaching life skills - a fact about an ancient literary work, so LO-161.
Sanskrit as the Panchatantra's original language; again a fact about the work rather than about its spread.
Defines an epic as a long heroic narrative poem - the literary category of the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
Names India's two great epics; the short-answer twin of the multiple-choice version, and again LO-161.
